copy.After “Check routing and deployment”; ap: Open a nested page by pasting its full URL into a fresh browser tab, then refresh it. Follow the same route from the homepage and compare the result. If navigation works but the direct load fails, investigate the deployed route and hosting fallback before rewriting the page. Also open a URL that does not exist and confirm it shows the intended missing-page response.
copy.After “Check forms and data handoff”; ap: Run one valid submission and confirm the saved lead reaches its intended destination. Then submit an invalid form and simulate a failed request in a test environment. The page should explain what failed, preserve useful input and let the visitor retry. Hold launch if the primary form loses leads or a required route fails. Put minor visual refinements on a follow-up list once the visitor can complete the page’s main task.

copy.“Common signs” paragraph; update its dup: The page looks fine at one width but breaks at another: sticky headers cover content, columns stack badly, buttons drift out of place, images extend beyond their containers, or an unwanted horizontal scrollbar appears.
copy.First two items in the pre-edit checklis: Record the affected URL, viewport and missing or altered CSS file before changing settings. Compare the page with cache bypassed, then purge the relevant cache if stale output is confirmed. On staging, change one optimization setting at a time-such as CSS combination or critical CSS-and retest the same viewport before moving to the next setting.

Compare the same URL in a clean browser session and while logged in. If only the public version is wrong, check cached output and any differences for logged-out visitors. If one page is wrong, compare its template, builder settings and content with a working page. If the change affects the whole site, record recent plugin, theme and PHP changes, then use a backup and staging copy to isolate the suspected component. Keep the test narrow enough to identify which change restores the expected behavior.

copy.Opening paragraph after the introductory: A page can look broken because its styles are wrong, its scripts never update the page, or both. Start with the action that fails. If the menu changes to its open state but remains hidden, inspect its styles. If the click never reaches the control, check for an overlay before tracing the event handler. If a request fails, follow that request before changing the layout.

css-javascript-errors-website-bugs.meta: Work out whether a broken menu, form or layout comes from CSS, JavaScript, an overlay or a failed request, then follow the right troubleshooting steps.

First inspect the iframe element and its wrapper on your own page. Width, spacing and overflow there can be corrected in the host layout. Content inside a frame from another origin is controlled by that provider; the parent page generally cannot reach in and restyle it. Use the provider’s responsive settings or supported resize integration when the embedded document itself needs to change. Retest the smallest phone width and the longest expected content before choosing a fixed height.
copy.Immediately after “Practical fix path”;: If the frame is blank Check Console and Network for the frame URL. A missing page, login redirect or refused embedding message needs a different fix from overflow. Record the exact message and check the provider’s supported embed URL and settings before changing the host layout.

copy.Opening explanatory paragraph beginning: Before changing a broken website, capture what fails and protect the current state. A failed form, stuck checkout, broken layout and inaccessible admin screen need different repairs, but the first rule is the same: preserve the evidence, identify the affected business path and make one reversible change at a time.
copy.After “Check the change timeline”; add a: Example: the form failed after a plugin update Record the old and new plugin versions and reproduce the failure on a staging copy. If reverting that plugin restores the form, check the plugin’s rollback guidance and any database changes before applying the recovery to the live site. A full database restore may remove orders or leads received after the backup. Choose the narrowest recovery that restores the form, then verify a new submission reaches its destination.

links.text: WordPress broken after a plugin update

If the modal never opens, inspect the click target, overlays and browser errors before changing email settings. If the form cannot send a request, check validation and JavaScript. If a request is sent, read its response: a 200 status alone does not prove the submission was accepted. Then check for the saved entry. An accepted entry with no notification points to email delivery; an entry and email with no CRM record points to the integration. Record the first missing step and its test time before changing the next system.
copy.Generic “API & Integrations” service car: Website Integration Help Use this when the form accepts a submission but the lead, fields or confirmation fail to reach the CRM, email system or other destination.

copy.“Reality checks” list item and the parag: Tag Assistant verifies the intended conversion action. A successful tag test and an attributed Google Ads conversion answer different questions. First verify the tag on the real success path. Then check whether the reported conversion has an eligible ad interaction, falls within the conversion window and is being compared using the intended report dates. Allow for processing delays. A direct test visit can verify the tag without producing an Ads-attributed conversion.
copy.“Check GA4 imports separately”; append a: If a native Google Ads tag and a GA4 import both represent the same lead, review which action the campaign uses for bidding. Keep the intended optimization action clear and use the other for comparison when appropriate. Check custom goals too: an action included in a custom goal can be used for bidding even when it is labeled secondary.

Button click: track as a separate interaction; count a lead only after confirmed submission success.
copy.FAQ answer to “Should I track a button c: Track a button click as a separate interaction. Count a submitted lead only after the form confirms success. Test validation failures, server errors and repeated clicks to make sure they do not generate lead events.
copy.After “Choose the right GTM trigger”; in: Example: an AJAX form with a success callback After the server confirms that the form was accepted, have the form’s supported success callback push a lead_form_success event to the data layer. Use that custom event as the GTM trigger for a GA4 generate_lead event. Send a form identifier, such as quote_request, rather than the visitor’s answers. In preview, submit once successfully and once with invalid data. The lead event should fire once for the successful submission and remain absent for the rejected one.

copy.First explanatory paragraph after the in: A menu will not open, a form never finishes, or a widget works only after a refresh. Reproduce that exact action, then use Console and Network to find the first failure that explains it.
copy.Paragraph beginning “This page is a focu: Still deciding whether the problem is CSS or JavaScript? Use the CSS and JavaScript diagnosis guide first. Continue here when a click, event, request or script fails to produce the expected result.
copy.After the paragraph that identifies the: Example: a menu click throws a TypeError Reproduce the click with Console open. Follow the error to its source, then pause at that line in Sources and inspect the value the code tries to use. If the menu element is null, compare the selector with the current markup and check whether the element exists when the script runs. A changed selector calls for a selector or markup fix; an element created later calls for an initialization fix. Retest the same click after the smallest change, including a fresh page load and the affected mobile width.

copy.“A page needs more than a headline and b: A short page can work when it gives the visitor enough information to understand the offer and take the next step. Start with a clear heading, an accurate offer, the intended audience and a working action. Add proof, process details or FAQs when they answer a real decision question. Choose the sections for the page’s purpose, then check the mobile layout, metadata, links and measurement before launch.
copy.“What makes a page good enough to launch: Hold launch if the offer is wrong, the main action fails, required routes do not load, or the mobile layout prevents someone from using the page. For a lead page, submit the form and confirm the lead arrives; for a campaign that depends on conversion reporting, verify the intended event under the tested consent settings. Once those checks pass, schedule smaller visual refinements and supporting content separately.

copy.Replace the “Proof example: audit notes: Turn one audit finding into a testable task Suppose an audit finds a service page pointing its canonical to the homepage. First confirm that the service page should be available as a separate search result. If it should, fix the canonical at the template or page setting that generated it, then check the live HTML and the preferred URL used in internal links and the sitemap. Record the before-and-after output. Search Console can later show Google’s selected canonical; changing the tag alone does not prove that selection changed.
copy.After “Not every SEO recommendation is e: For example, an unintended noindex on a service page needs investigation before rewriting that page’s description. Confirm that the page is meant to appear in search, remove the blocking directive at its source and check the live response. A description rewrite can improve the snippet proposal, but it cannot make a page blocked by noindex eligible for indexing.

copy.After the WooCommerce Checkout Error Fix: What I would keep separate WooCommerce Support and Checkout Error Fix Help have a page-to-page cosine of 0.855, and the published passages already link them in both directions. Their jobs remain different: broad store work on one page, a failed purchase path on the other. I would keep both pages and those contextual links. The phrase “woocommerce broken checkout checker” shows why meaning alone is insufficient. Its vector fit is 75.84, while its combined score is 41.77; the wording may ask for a tool even though the page offers hands-on diagnosis. I would keep the repair page focused on the checkout failures I check and the work the service delivers. A checker or monitoring product would need its own real offering before it deserved a promise on that page.
copy.Opening paragraph under “Three pages wit: An empty returned query list does not establish zero search visibility. Search Console omits some queries for privacy and does not show every row. Check the page-level performance data before treating an empty query list as zero impressions. Here, the absence means there is no disclosed page-query pair to score.

List each place tracking is installed: GTM, theme code, a CMS plugin, an ecommerce integration or a vendor widget. Record the destination ID and the action each installation sends. Then perform one successful test action under the consent choice being tested. Compare the event name, destination and number of sends. Two requests are not automatically duplicates; two copies of the same business event sent to the same destination are the issue to investigate.
If the form itself fails, start with forms and modals not working. If the lead arrives but the event is missing or duplicated, use the GTM form tracking guide. If the tag fires but Google Ads reporting still looks wrong, follow the Google Ads conversion tracking checks.
copy.“Common symptoms” sentence, including it: GA4 events or key events are missing, GTM shows unexpected tag activity, the same event fires twice, or ad-platform totals disagree with recorded leads and orders.

copy.Flow displayed after “Data problems usua: From one accepted form submission, trace both paths: Lead delivery: accepted form → saved entry → email or CRM. Measurement: confirmed success → GTM event → GA4 → report. Compare the form identity and test time at each step. The first missing or changed record tells you which handoff to inspect.
copy.Replace “Proof example: one action, ever: Follow one test lead Suppose the form saves an entry and sends the confirmation email, but the CRM record is missing a required field. Compare that field in the saved entry, outgoing payload and CRM response. If the payload omits it, fix the field mapping before changing the analytics tag. If the payload includes it but the CRM rejects it, inspect the destination field name and validation rules. Retest with controlled data and keep personal form contents out of analytics.
If the form never accepts a submission, start with forms and modals not working. If the lead reaches the CRM but GA4 misses it, use the GTM form tracking guide. For a failed connection that needs repair, Website Integration Help covers the handoff between the site and the destination system.

copy.“Look for script, cache, and session iss: Identify whether the page uses classic checkout or the Checkout block. In Network, preserve the log and inspect Fetch/XHR while reproducing the failure. Classic checkout commonly uses wc-ajax requests; the Checkout block uses WooCommerce Store API requests. Record the failing URL, status, response and test time. Before retrying payment, check whether an order or charge already exists. A spinner can remain even after the server has accepted part of the checkout.
copy.“Verify order data and tracking after th: For a test in which the intended consent settings permit measurement, compare the order ID, currency, value and items with the purchase event sent to the intended analytics property. Check for a second purchase event after refreshing the confirmation page. Record the consent choice with the test so an intentionally restricted measurement path is not diagnosed as a broken checkout.

copy.“Recover carefully”; insert after its op: If the dashboard will not open Check the WordPress administrator inbox and spam folder for a Recovery Mode email. Its link can let you sign in with the failing component paused for that session, and the message may identify the plugin or theme involved. Record that name, the error and the updated version. If no email arrives, ask the host for the relevant PHP error log and recovery help; a missing email does not rule out a fatal error.
copy.“Recover carefully”; add before the safe: Before choosing rollback or restore, check what the update changed. Reverting plugin files may leave a database migration in place. Restoring an older database can remove newer orders, leads or edits. Confirm the plugin’s rollback guidance and the backup timestamp, then choose a recovery path that preserves current business records. Retest the original failure after recovery.
